verses.commentary: The word of the Lord came. Standard prophetic formula, but what follows is anything but standard. Jonah son of Amittai appears in 2 Kings 14:25 as a prophet during Jeroboam II's reign, predicting Israel's expansion. Now God sends him to Israel's enemy.

Nineveh, capital of Assyria, the terror of the ancient Near East. Israel's destroyer within a generation. God sends his prophet not to condemn from afar but to preach in person. The mission seems suicidal, the mercy incomprehensible.

Jonah runs. Tarshish lies at the western edge of the known world, likely Spain. Maximum distance from Nineveh to the east. The text repeats: from the Lord, from the Lord. He flees not the mission but the Missionary. Down to Joppa, down into the ship. Descent begins.
The Lord hurls a great wind. The same verb used later when the sailors hurl cargo and Jonah into the sea. God enters the chase. Creation itself pursues the fugitive prophet.

Pagan sailors pray while God's prophet sleeps. Bitter irony. They lighten the ship; he weighs it down with his rebellion. Each cries to his god; Jonah remains silent. The prophet has become the problem.

A pagan captain rebukes a Hebrew prophet. Call on your god! The one man who knows the true God refuses to pray. Role reversal exposes Jonah's spiritual condition. He who should lead in prayer must be commanded to it.
Lots reveal what prayer could not. Ancient practice, but God governs even random chance (Proverbs 16:33). The lot falls on Jonah. Providence will not let him hide.
Five rapid questions. The sailors want to understand what cosmic force they have offended. Work, origin, country, people. They sense this is bigger than one man's bad luck.

I am a Hebrew. Jonah confesses his identity and his God. The God of heaven who made sea and dry land. He knows the theology perfectly. The creator of the very sea now raging controls all. Knowledge without obedience.
They knew he was running. Jonah had already told them. His confession matches his flight. The sailors, pagans, respond with appropriate fear. The prophet remains unmoved.
What should we do to you? They ask the prophet for prophetic guidance. Irony compounds. The man fleeing God's word must now speak it to save others.

Throw me into the sea. Jonah prefers death to obedience. He will sacrifice himself for the sailors but not preach to Nineveh. Selective compassion. He acknowledges his fault but still resists the mission.
The sailors try to spare him. Pagans show more mercy than the prophet of mercy. They row hard toward land, fighting the very sea Jonah's God commands. Futile but noble.

Now the sailors pray to Yahweh by name. They have learned more theology in one storm than Jonah has practiced in his ministry. Do not hold us accountable. They fear the guilt of blood. You, Lord, have done as you pleased. They recognize divine sovereignty.
They throw him in. The sea grows calm. Instant proof of Jonah's God. The storm was personal, targeted, purposeful. Now it stops.

The sailors fear the Lord greatly. They offer sacrifice and make vows. Conversion at sea. Pagans worship while the prophet sinks. The first Gentiles converted through Jonah's ministry, against his will.

The Lord appointed a great fish. Same verb as the wind, the plant, the worm, the east wind. God orchestrates creation for his purposes. Three days and three nights. Jesus claims this as a sign of his own death and resurrection (Matthew 12:40). The rebellious prophet becomes a type of the obedient Savior.
